title: Roebuck v. Mayo Clinic
description: Whether A.R.S. § 12-516(A) violates the Arizona Constitution's anti-abrogation clause by barring claims for ordinary negligence but allowing claims for wilful misconduct or gross negligence against health care providers delivering pandemic-related medical treatment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that A.R.S. § 12-516(A) unconstitutionally abrogates the right to sue for ordinary negligence, as gross negligence is not a reasonable alternative.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that A.R.S. § 12-516(A) provides immunity for ordinary negligence in COVID-19 treatment and merely regulates, rather than abrogates, the right to action by allowing claims for gross negligence.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's summary judgment in favor of Mayo Clinic, concluding that A.R.S. § 12-516(A) unconstitutionally abrogates the right to sue for ordinary negligence, and remanded the case.

title: Roundtree v. City of Page
description: Whether an initiative proposed by residents of the City of Page, which seeks to prevent the narrowing of a specific street, is legislative in nature and therefore falls within the citizens' right to initiate laws at the local level.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the initiative is legislative in nature, creating policy and a permanent rule, and thus falls within citizens' right to initiate laws, or alternatively, that the constitution authorizes initiatives on any matter, not just legislation.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the initiative is administrative, not legislative, as it merely implements existing City policy and supplants administrative authority, and therefore is not a valid subject for a citizen initiative.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' decision and reversed the trial court's decision, ruling that the proposed initiative is legislative in nature and can proceed to the ballot.

title: Smith v. Fontes
description: Whether A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A), which mandates double counting of some invalid signatures for initiative petitions, is unconstitutional as applied because it effectively raises the constitutional 15% signature threshold, thereby hindering the ability of initiatives to qualify for the ballot.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs challenged the 'Make Elections Fair Act' initiative's eligibility for the ballot, arguing it failed to meet constitutional signature requirements and that the statute's application should have disqualified it.
defendant_argument: The defendants, specifically Make Elections Fair PAC, argued that A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A) was unconstitutional as applied because its double counting mechanism effectively raised the 15% signature threshold, and without this unconstitutional application, the Initiative would have qualified.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment dismissing the challenge to the Initiative, ruling that A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A) was unconstitutional as applied because it impermissibly raised the signature threshold, thus allowing the Initiative to qualify for the ballot.

title: Knight v. Fontes
description: Whether the geographic voting districts for court of appeals judges, as defined by A.R.S. § 12-120.02, violate the Free and Equal Elections Clause and the Equal Privileges and Immunities Clause of the Arizona Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing they do and defendants arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: The geographic voting districts disenfranchise voters and give unequal weight to votes, arguing that statewide jurisdiction of the court of appeals mandates statewide retention elections.
defendant_argument: The statute is constitutional, as there is no underlying right to vote in every court of appeals judge's retention election, and the one-person, one-vote principle does not apply to the judiciary.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's order dismissing the plaintiffs' claim, ruling that the retention election process for court of appeals judges is constitutional.

title: Sync Title Agency, LLC v. Arizona Corporation Commission
description: Whether Sync Title Agency, LLC, is liable for selling unregistered securities and committing securities fraud, with the plaintiff arguing for a non-public offering exemption and against fraud findings, and the defendant arguing against the exemption and for the fraud findings.
plaintiff_argument: Sync argued that the sale of membership interest was an exempt non-public offering, that it had a constitutional right to a jury trial for alleged securities fraud violations, and that the Commission's findings of securities fraud were not supported by substantial evidence.
defendant_argument: The Arizona Corporation Commission argued that Sync sold an unregistered, non-exempt security and committed securities fraud through misrepresentations and omissions, and that Arizona law does not grant a jury-trial right for Commission enforcement actions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part, vacating the Commission's order in part, and remanded the case for proceedings consistent with its decision. It found Sync participated in the sale, denied a jury trial right, but concluded the offering was exempt from registration. It also found some fraud claims were puffery or had a reasonable basis, but upheld the fraud finding regarding the personal use of investment funds.

title: Francisco v. Affiliated Urologists
description: Whether an FDA black box warning regarding prescription medication can serve to establish the standard of care and obviate the need for expert testimony in medical malpractice cases, with the plaintiffs arguing it can and the defendants arguing it cannot.
plaintiff_argument: The Franciscos argued that expert testimony was not necessary because a jury could understand FDA warnings and their materiality, and that requiring expert testimony when no board-certified urologist would testify due to AUA guidance violated the anti-abrogation clause.
defendant_argument: The Practice argued that expert medical testimony is required to establish the standard of care in medical malpractice claims, and FDA warnings alone are insufficient because medical judgment is involved.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' decision and affirmed the trial court's judgment, ruling that FDA black box warnings cannot substitute for expert testimony to establish the standard of care in medical malpractice cases.

title: Gilpin v. Harris
description: Whether defendants adjudicated 'guilty except insane' (GEI) are criminally responsible for their actions and thus liable for victim restitution.
plaintiff_argument: Lisa Gilpin, as a victim, argued that Marcos Martinez, a GEI defendant, should pay restitution under Arizona's Victims' Bill of Rights, asserting that GEI defendants are criminally responsible.
defendant_argument: Marcos Martinez argued that a GEI judgment is not a 'conviction' for restitution purposes, and therefore restitution was unavailable, relying on the precedent set in State v. Heartfield.
decision_outcome: The court overruled the precedent set in State v. Heartfield and held that restitution is available from defendants adjudged 'guilty except insane' when their actions caused or threatened death or serious injury, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Gilmore v. Gallego
description: Whether "release time" provisions in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the City of Phoenix and a union violate free-speech, free-association, right-to-work rights, or the Gift Clause of the Arizona Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the release time provisions violate their free-speech, free-association, and right-to-work rights, and also violate the Gift Clause, especially if the City pays for it.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the release time provisions do not violate free-speech, free-association, or right-to-work rights because the City pays for them, and do not violate the Gift Clause because they serve a public purpose and are supported by adequate consideration.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the release time provisions do not violate free-speech, free-association, or right-to-work rights, but they do violate the Gift Clause of the Arizona Constitution, remanding the case for judgment in favor of the Employees on the Gift Clause claim.

title: Pima County. v. State
description: Whether the State must reimburse Pima County for desegregation expenses that exceed the Arizona Constitution's 1% Limit on residential property taxes as "additional state aid for education" following the 2018 legislative amendments to A.R.S. § 15-910, and whether these taxes continue to be "primary property taxes" eligible for reimbursement.
plaintiff_argument: The State must reimburse Pima County for desegregation expenses because the 2018 amendments to § 15-910 are unworkable, do not trump constitutional limitations, and do not eliminate the State's reimbursement obligation for primary property taxes.
defendant_argument: The State is not obligated to reimburse Pima County because the 2018 amendments reclassified desegregation expenses as a new type of secondary property tax, which is not eligible for state reimbursement under § 15-972(E), and these amendments are constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the State is not obligated to reimburse Pima County for desegregation expenses, affirming the court of appeals' opinion.

title: Mitchell v. Palmer
description: Whether a prosecutor's office should be disqualified when a crime victim works in the same office responsible for prosecuting the individual accused of the crime, and what factors a trial court should consider in such a decision.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Arizona (petitioner) argued that the trial court erred by not applying the Gomez factors when disqualifying the Maricopa County Attorney's Office (MCAO) and that MCAO's screening procedures were adequate to prevent conflict.
defendant_argument: Tamira Marie Durand (real party in interest) argued that her due process rights would be violated if she were prosecuted by an agency with a conflict of interest, specifically because the victim was an employee of MCAO.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's order disqualifying the Maricopa County Attorney's Office and remanded the case for the trial court to apply the Gomez factors and consider Durand's due process rights.

title: Neptune Swimming Foundation v. City of Scottsdale
description: Whether the City of Scottsdale violated the Gift Clause by not considering a higher bid when awarding a license and whether it abused its discretion by canceling a Request for Proposal (RFP) process.
plaintiff_argument: Neptune argued the City violated the Gift Clause by awarding a license at below-market rates and abused its discretion by canceling the RFP and not awarding the license to Neptune, the most advantageous bidder.
defendant_argument: The City argued it did not violate the Gift Clause, as a higher bid is not conclusive for fair market value, and it did not abuse its discretion by canceling the RFP and extending an existing license.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed summary judgment for the City on the Gift Clause claim, finding no violation, but reversed summary judgment for the City on the procurement code claim, remanding for further proceedings to determine if the City abused its discretion.

title: Cao v. PFP Dorsey Investments
description: Whether the Arizona Condominium Act, specifically § 33-1228(C), authorized the forced sale of individual condominium units rather than the entire condominium property, and whether the statute as applied violated the eminent domain provision of the Arizona Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Xias argued that the forced sale of their unit violated § 33-1228(C) because it prohibited the forced sale of less than an entire condominium, and alternatively, that § 33-1228 was unconstitutional as it authorized a taking of private property for private use.
defendant_argument: PFP Dorsey Investments, LLC, and the Association argued that the sale complied with § 33-1228 and that the Xias contractually agreed to the terms of the Declaration, which incorporated the Condominium Act.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' decision, affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the eminent domain claim, but reversed on the interpretation of § 33-1228(C), holding that it authorized only the sale of all condominium property, not individual units, if a forced sale occurred. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

title: State v. Santillanes
description: Whether the State has the right to appeal a trial court's order granting expungement and restoration of civil rights, or whether it may seek relief only through a petition for special action.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued it has the right to appeal expungement orders under A.R.S. § 13-4032(4) because such orders affect its substantial rights.
defendant_argument: Santillanes argued that A.R.S. § 36-2862(F) provides the exclusive grounds for appeal in expungement cases, allowing only petitioners to appeal denials, and that an expungement order does not affect the State's substantial rights.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the State has the right to appeal an order expunging records pertaining to a felony conviction and restoring civil rights under A.R.S. § 13-4032(4), vacating parts of the court of appeals' opinion and remanding for further proceedings.

title: Planned Parenthood of Arizona v. Hazelrigg
description: Whether the Arizona Legislature repealed or otherwise restricted A.R.S. § 13-3603, a near-total abortion ban, by enacting A.R.S. § 36-2322, which proscribes physicians from performing elective abortions after fifteen weeks' gestation.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argued that A.R.S. § 36-2322 implicitly authorizes abortions up to fifteen weeks' gestation and in medical emergencies, thereby repealing or restricting A.R.S. § 13-3603, and that the statutes should be harmonized.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General and intervenors argued that A.R.S. § 36-2322 does not create an independent right to abortion or repeal A.R.S. § 13-3603, and that with Roe v. Wade overturned, A.R.S. § 13-3603 is now fully enforceable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment vacating the injunction of A.R.S. § 13-3603, making the near-total abortion ban enforceable, and vacated the court of appeals' opinion.

title: Torres v. Jai Dining Services
description: Whether the anti-abrogation clause extends to dram-shop actions recognized after statehood, thereby preventing the legislature from limiting such actions.
plaintiff_argument: The anti-abrogation clause protects the common law dram-shop action, which evolved from pre-statehood negligence rights, and thus the legislature cannot limit it.
defendant_argument: The anti-abrogation clause does not protect dram-shop actions because they were created after statehood, allowing the legislature to limit them.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the anti-abrogation clause does not protect dram-shop actions because they were recognized after statehood, thus affirming the legislature's ability to limit such actions and ruling in favor of JAI Dining Services.

title: Draper v. Gentry
description: Whether a defendant must satisfy a 'reasonable possibility' or 'substantial probability' standard to compel the extraction of GPS data from a crime victim's vehicle for their defense, balancing the defendant's right to a complete defense against the victim's constitutional and statutory privacy rights.
plaintiff_argument: Lane Draper argued that compelling the extraction of GPS data from his truck violated his constitutional rights against unreasonable search and seizure (Fourth Amendment), his state constitutional privacy rights, and his rights as a victim under the Victims' Bill of Rights.
defendant_argument: Jordon Nez argued that his due process right to present a complete defense, including a third-party defense implicating Draper, required access to Draper's GPS data, and that the 'reasonable possibility' standard should apply.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's order and remanded the case, establishing a conditional standard for compelling GPS data extraction from a crime victim's vehicle, requiring a 'reasonable possibility' for in-camera review with safeguards and a 'substantial probability' for direct disclosure.

title: State v. Purcell
description: Whether the court of appeals had appellate jurisdiction over the dismissal of resentencing proceedings for juvenile offenders, with petitioners arguing for jurisdiction and the state arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the resentencing proceedings were not post-conviction relief (PCR) proceedings and that the trial court's orders affected their substantial rights, thus granting the court of appeals jurisdiction for a direct appeal.
defendant_argument: The state argued that the proceedings were PCR proceedings, and therefore, appellate review required a petition for review, not a direct appeal, meaning the court of appeals lacked jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Arizona concluded that the court of appeals had jurisdiction over the appeals in these cases and remanded them for further consideration.

title: State v. Brearcliffe
description: Whether § 13-4033(C) requires a defendant to receive prior notice and an opportunity at sentencing to prove that their absence was involuntary before their right to appeal can be divested.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Phillip Johnson waived his right to appeal under § 13-4033(C) and that the court of appeals erred by requiring specific findings for waiver, implying that notice and opportunity to prove involuntary absence were not strictly required by the statute for waiver.
defendant_argument: Phillip Johnson argued that § 13-4033(C) requires prior notice and an opportunity at sentencing to prove that his absence was involuntary, and also that the statute itself was unconstitutional as it usurps the Court's rulemaking authority.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals' order and remanded the case to the trial court to provide Johnson an opportunity to prove by clear and convincing evidence that his absence was involuntary.

title: Matthews v. The Industrial Commission of Arizona
description: Whether A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B), which limits workers' compensation claims for mental illnesses to those arising from an "unexpected, unusual or extraordinary stress" situation, violates article 18, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution or the equal protection guarantee of article 2, section 13.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B) unconstitutionally restricts workers' compensation for mental injuries by treating them differently than physical injuries, violating Article 18, Section 8 of the Arizona Constitution and equal protection guarantees.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B) is constitutional because the original Workers' Compensation Act did not encompass mental injuries, and the legislature has the prerogative to define and expand workers' compensation coverage within limits.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the decision of the court of appeals, upholding the constitutionality of A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B) and affirming the ALJ's award determination that the plaintiff's mental injury claim was non-compensable.

title: Burns v. Arizona Public Service Co.
description: Whether the Arizona Constitution allows a majority of commissioners to prevent any single commissioner from exercising investigatory powers expressly granted to each in article 15, section 4.
plaintiff_argument: Robert Burns argued that individual commissioners have the constitutional and statutory authority to inspect and investigate public service corporations and issue subpoenas without the approval of other commissioners.
defendant_argument: Arizona Public Service Company and the Commission argued that the Commission as a body, not individual commissioners, holds the authority to enforce investigatory powers, especially in ratemaking cases, and can quash subpoenas if deemed unreasonable or oppressive.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' opinion, reversed the superior court's denial of summary judgment, and remanded the case, ruling that a majority of commissioners cannot prevent an individual commissioner from exercising their investigatory powers.

title: Leibsohn v. Hobbs
description: Whether signatures collected by initiative petition circulators must be disqualified due to failure to strictly comply with statutory registration requirements, specifically regarding residence addresses and multiple affidavits.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that signatures should be disqualified because circulators failed to strictly comply with statutory requirements for listing a unit number in their residence address and submitting a new affidavit for each petition.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that a unit number is not explicitly required for a residence address and that one affidavit for multiple initiative measures complies, especially since the Secretary of State's electronic system prevented uploading multiple affidavits.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, refusing to disqualify signatures, concluding that the Secretary of State's registration procedures made it impossible for circulators to comply with the affidavit requirement, and that disqualifying signatures would unconstitutionally hinder the initiative process.

title: Arizona Free Enterprise Club v. Hobbs
description: Whether tax revenue measures, specifically Senate Bill 1828, are exempt from the referendum power under the Arizona Constitution's 'support and maintenance' clause, even if they decrease revenue.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that SB 1828 is exempt from the referendum process under the Arizona Constitution's 'support and maintenance' clause, and that the referendum petition was statutorily deficient.
defendant_argument: The defendant contended that SB 1828 was referable to the voters because it did not qualify as a 'support and maintenance' measure, arguing that only appropriation measures, not revenue provisions, are exempt, and that a tax measure must increase revenue to be exempt.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's order, ruling that SB 1828 is exempt from the referendum process.

title: Fann v. Kemp
description: Whether the Arizona Senate's communications regarding its 2020 election audit are protected by legislative privilege from public disclosure, with American Oversight arguing for disclosure and the Senate arguing for privilege.
plaintiff_argument: American Oversight argued that the Senate's audit communications were public records subject to disclosure, not protected by legislative privilege, and that any privilege was waived by public statements.
defendant_argument: The Senate asserted that its audit of the 2020 election was a privileged legislative act, and therefore, its internal communications regarding the audit were protected by legislative privilege.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's order, ruling that legislative privilege applies to the Senate's audit communications concerning legislative activities, but not to administrative or political matters, and remanded for the Senate to provide a more specific privilege log.

title: Willis v. Bernini
description: Whether a person under grand jury investigation has a due process right to a fair and impartial presentation of clearly exculpatory evidence, and whether a prosecutor has a duty to present such evidence, including evidence relevant to a justification defense, to a grand jury.
plaintiff_argument: Willis argued that the State withheld clearly exculpatory evidence of a justification defense, which it was obligated to present even without a specific request.
defendant_argument: The State contended it complied with its obligations, did not withhold exculpatory evidence, and asserted there is no constitutional due process right to a fair and impartial presentation of evidence before a grand jury.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's ruling concerning Willis' 12.9 Motion and remanded the case with instructions to send it back to the grand jury for a redetermination of probable cause.

title: State v. Robinson
description: Whether Dwandarrius Jamar Robinson's convictions and death sentences should be affirmed despite his challenges regarding jury selection, aggravating circumstances, jury instructions, and prosecutorial conduct.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the trial court correctly handled jury selection, that aggravating circumstances were proven beyond a reasonable doubt, that jury instructions were proper, and that there was no prosecutorial misconduct, thus affirming Robinson's convictions and sentences.
defendant_argument: Robinson argued that his convictions and sentences should be overturned due to errors in jury selection, insufficient evidence for aggravating circumstances, flawed jury instructions regarding life imprisonment, an unconstitutional capital sentencing scheme, and prosecutorial misconduct.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Dwandarrius Jamar Robinson's convictions and sentences for first-degree murder, arson, and kidnapping.

title: State v. Reed
description: Whether a victim's attorney fees are recoverable as criminal restitution and, if so, to what extent.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the attorney fees were a direct result of Reed's criminal conduct and thus properly ordered as restitution.
defendant_argument: The petitioners argued that the attorney fees were consequential damages, not directly caused by Reed's criminal conduct, and therefore not recoverable as restitution.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's restitution order for most of C.C.'s attorney fees, finding them to be indirect consequential damages, but remanded for a determination on two specific billing entries.

title: Arizona School Boards Association,  Inc. v. State
description: Whether four legislative budget reconciliation bills (HB 2898, SB 1824, SB 1825, and SB 1819) violate the Arizona Constitution's "title requirement" or "single subject rule."
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that all four budget reconciliation bills violated the title requirement, and that SB 1819 also violated the single subject rule, rendering them unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the budget reconciliation bills' titles satisfied the title requirement, that the bills complied with constitutional standards, and that the plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge SB 1819, presenting a non-justiciable political question.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, ruling that the challenged sections of HB 2898, SB 1824, SB 1825, and SB 1819 violated the title requirement and that SB 1819 entirely violated the single subject rule, rendering those sections and SB 1819 unconstitutional and void.

title: Fay v. Fox
description: Whether a crime victim has a constitutional and statutory right to be heard on the merits of a defendant's motion for a delayed appeal of a restitution order, with the plaintiff arguing for this right and the defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Beth Fay, argued that she has a constitutional and statutory right to be heard on the defendant's motion for a delayed appeal of a restitution order because it implicates her rights to due process, prompt restitution, and finality, and could delay or extinguish her restitution award.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Jordan Michael Hanson, argued that victims do not have a general right to be heard in post-conviction relief proceedings, or specifically on claims for permission to take a delayed appeal from a Criminal Restitution Order, unless such a right is expressly provided by law.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals decision and reversed the trial court judgment, holding that a crime victim has a constitutional and statutory right to be heard on the merits of a Rule 32.1(f) motion for a delayed appeal to contest a restitution award.

title: Fann v. State
description: Whether Proposition 208, a voter initiative imposing an income tax surcharge for education funding, violates the Education Expenditure Clause by purporting to exempt its funds from expenditure limitations and whether it violates the Tax Enactment Clause by imposing a new tax without a legislative supermajority vote.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Karen Fann, argued that Proposition 208's direct funding to schools violates the Education Expenditure Clause and that it unconstitutionally imposes a new tax without the supermajority vote required by the Tax Enactment Clause.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Invest in Arizona, argued that Proposition 208 funds are 'grants' exempt from the Education Expenditure Clause and that the Tax Enactment Clause does not apply to voter initiatives. They also contended the case was not ripe for decision.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of a preliminary injunction against Proposition 208, ruled that the Tax Enactment Clause does not apply to voter initiatives, but found Proposition 208's direct funding unconstitutional to the extent it mandates spending in violation of the Education Expenditure Clause and that these provisions are not severable, remanding the case to the trial court to determine if revenues will exceed the expenditure limit.

title: Redgrave v. Ducey
description: Whether Arizona has consented to damages liability for a state agency's violation of the minimum wage or overtime provisions of the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA).
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Arizona has waived its sovereign immunity to FLSA claims, either by removing the case to federal court or as a matter of law, and that the rule favoring government liability extends to federal damages claims.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Arizona legislature has not unequivocally consented to federal damages liability, and therefore, the state retains its sovereign immunity under the FLSA.
decision_outcome: The court held that Arizona has not consented to damages liability for a state agency's violation of the FLSA's minimum wage or overtime provisions because the legislature has not expressly or unequivocally implied such consent.

title: State v. Bigger
description: Whether a defendant must present a standard of care expert affidavit to support an ineffective assistance of counsel (IAC) claim, whether Perry v. New Hampshire caused a significant change in Arizona law, and whether A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) supplements rather than conflicts with Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.4 regarding post-conviction relief filing deadlines.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Ronald Bruce Bigger, argued that he received ineffective assistance of counsel, that Perry v. New Hampshire constituted a significant change in the law entitling him to relief, and that A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) unconstitutionally conflicts with Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.4.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Arizona, argued that Bigger's ineffective assistance of counsel claims were not proven, that Perry v. New Hampshire did not cause a significant change in Arizona law, and implicitly that A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) was constitutional or supplemental to court rules.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals' opinion and affirmed the trial court's ruling dismissing Bigger's post-conviction relief petition, finding no expert affidavit is required for IAC claims, Perry did not change Arizona law, and A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) unconstitutionally conflicts with court rules.

title: Mesnard v. Campagnolo
description: Whether a legislator is absolutely immune from liability for defamation when modifying an investigatory report and issuing a news release, under the legislative immunity doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: Mesnard argued he was absolutely immune from defamation liability for both the investigatory report and the news release because these actions constituted legislative functions.
defendant_argument: Shooter argued Mesnard was not immune because his actions, particularly the modifications to the report and the news release, were not legitimate legislative functions and denied due process.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's denial of Mesnard's motion to dismiss regarding the news release, but reversed the denial of dismissal regarding the investigatory report, remanding for further proceedings on the news release claims.

title: State v. Patel
description: Whether A.R.S. § 28-672(G), which limits the amount of restitution that can be awarded to a victim for loss resulting from a violation of specified traffic offenses, is either an unconstitutional limitation on the right to receive restitution or a valid legislative enactment.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Victims' Bill of Rights (VBR) guarantees a right to full restitution, and the statutory limitation was unconstitutional as it conflicted with this constitutional right.
defendant_argument: Patel argued that the VBR's plain language does not require "full" restitution, and the legislature has the authority to limit restitution amounts.
decision_outcome: The court held that the constitutional right to receive restitution guaranteed by the VBR is a right to receive the full amount of economic loss or injury caused by a defendant's criminal conduct, and therefore, § 28-672(G)'s limitation on a restitution award is unconstitutional and void, reinstating the municipal court's restitution order of $61,191.99.

title: State ex rel. Brnovich v. City of Tucson
description: Whether Arizona Revised Statutes § 16-204.01, which mandates consolidating local elections with state and national elections when voter turnout decreases, can apply to a charter city whose charter requires electing local officials on non-statewide election dates.
plaintiff_argument: The state law § 16-204.01 should apply to the City of Tucson because increasing voter turnout in local elections is a matter of statewide concern, and low turnout adversely affects the fundamental right to vote and electoral integrity.
defendant_argument: The City of Tucson's charter provision requiring off-cycle elections is a matter of purely municipal concern, and the state law cannot preempt its local autonomy in structuring its government.
decision_outcome: The court held that Arizona Revised Statutes § 16-204.01 is unconstitutional as applied to the City of Tucson's charter, allowing the city to continue holding off-cycle municipal elections.

title: Schires v. Carlat
description: Whether the City of Peoria violated the Arizona Constitution's Gift Clause by spending public funds to induce a private university to open a branch campus.
plaintiff_argument: The City's payments to a private university and developer violated the Gift Clause because the public benefits were indirect and the value received by the public was far exceeded by the payments, constituting an impermissible subsidy.
defendant_argument: The City's payments served a public purpose by stimulating economic development and diversifying the economic base, and the value received by the public, including anticipated tax revenue and economic impact, was not far exceeded by the payments.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the lower court's judgment, ruling that the City of Peoria violated the Gift Clause by providing public funds to a private university and developer.

title: State v. Mixton
description: Whether the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution or article 2, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution requires law enforcement officials to secure a judicially-authorized search warrant or order to obtain a user's Internet Protocol (IP) address or subscriber information voluntarily provided to an Internet Service Provider (ISP), with the State arguing no warrant is required and Mixton arguing such information is protected.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that neither the federal nor the Arizona Constitution requires a search warrant or court order to obtain IP addresses and ISP subscriber information.
defendant_argument: Mixton argues that both the Fourth Amendment and the Arizona Constitution protect IP addresses and ISP subscriber information, requiring a search warrant or court order.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Mixton's convictions, holding that neither the Fourth Amendment nor article 2, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution requires a search warrant or court order for law enforcement to obtain IP addresses or ISP subscriber information, as this information is not considered a 'private affair' under the third-party doctrine.
